speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I welcome the scrutiny, the questions, because financial integrity and probity are critical for Singapore and for anyone standing up here.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Without that, we will be finished as a country.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And even though I had not factored in a Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB) interview as part of my job description, together with the caution, I believe it to be important.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As a member of the Government, it is important that I am held accountable to Singaporeans and to subject myself and this matter to scrutiny.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is how our system works and must continue to work.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: CPIB has investigated on whether I have had any unfair benefit.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is a key point, and I will come back to that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now answer some questions people have raised with me.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some of these questions relate to the choices I made, and which are very private.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Many will appreciate that the choice of a person's home is typically a personal and private matter.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I am mindful that as an elected official whose authority is conferred on me by the trust of Singaporeans, the lines between what is personal and public may not always be clear.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The questions I will deal with are: one, why am I living in a rented place in the first place and why am I not living in my own house; two, am I making some money renting out my own property while I live in a house rented from the state; three, the size of the land surrounding the Ridout house; four, what the Ridout house is like; and five, was there a conflict of interest?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am renting because I decided to put my family home, where I was living before June 2018, up for sale.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2016, I was approaching my 60s, age-wise.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I reviewed my finances and realised that too much of my savings were tied up in my family home.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I had bought the house using my previous income as a lawyer before I became a Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When I bought my family home, I had assumed a future stream of income, based on what I was earning in the private sector.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After I became a Minister, my income changed and thus I found too much of my savings was tied up in one house.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I was advised that it would be wiser not to have most of one's savings in one asset.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I decided to put my family home up for sale.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Before I proceed further, let me make it clear.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I did not consider selling my own home because of financial need.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I also do not regret having forgone my previous earnings as a Senior Counsel.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a privilege to be in public service and, if I am asked, I will make the same choice again.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, to prepare for the sale, I decided to move out from my family home and live in a rental property.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I looked at several rental properties, including black and white houses.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have long liked black and white houses.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And eventually, in 2018, I decided to make an offer for 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I told my agent to assess how much I should offer based on surrounding properties.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I told my agent I should not be paying less than what my neighbours paid, but I am not sure exactly when I told him that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I had no idea, when I accepted SLA's counter-offer, what the guide rent or the minimum rent was.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These were decisions internal to SLA that I was not privy to.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Around the same time, I also rented out my family home while deciding on the sale.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It took me a while to decide to sell, and then COVID-19 intervened.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My family home was put on the market in November 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will move to the second question now.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It has been asked, am I renting out my family home and, in turn, living at 26 Ridout Road so that I can make some money from the rental difference?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The first point – I am paying market rent for 26 Ridout Road and that is the critical point.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I am, in essence, using my previous lawyer's income to pay for the rental for 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Based on my current income, I would not have offered to rent 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is based on my personal approach to finances.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I should add, my family home, I think some people know, is a Good Class Bungalow (GCB).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I moved from there for the reasons that I have explained.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Indeed, I offered to maintain that land outside of the house boundary at my own cost, because if the outside land was not properly maintained, there would be serious problems for me.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But I did not want it as part of the lease.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My reason – if you own a landed property, you want a large land area.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But if you are a tenant, any land under your lease becomes your own responsibility and thus, an additional land area of 150,000 square feet means additional legal responsibility.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, there are large trees in the property.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If any of them fell, it could be serious.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2017, a tree fell on someone in the Botanic Gardens.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A person died, even though the tree had just been inspected and assessed to be healthy the year before.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The larger your land, the greater the responsibility for potential health risks, including mosquitoes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I did not need the land and did not want it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In fact, to explain my thinking, I will read out parts of an email which I sent to my agent, and I put up a draft for him to send to SLA.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It reads, "We have also been discussing the surrounding state land.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our client is concerned about the thick vegetation in the shaded area and the disamenities from that land, mosquitoes and very real likelihood of snakes.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will be other animals but that might be a lesser concern.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our client would like to propose that the undergrowth in the parts shaded yellow be cleared, leaving only matured trees.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our client will then be happy to maintain this area at his own cost.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will give him some comfort on the health and safety issues while it will save SLA the cost of maintenance of the land.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our client proposes that this arrangement be subject to termination with some notice, if either party finds it not feasible for any reason." The email was not sent in the end, because the contents were communicated at a meeting.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But SLA took the position that if I wanted to maintain the surrounding land, the surrounding land had to be part of the lease.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I did not want to negotiate and agreed to this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Even now, if SLA agrees to take back the extra land, which is more than 60% of the total, I would be extremely happy to give it up.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I would be happy to maintain it, if SLA agrees because that was what I wanted to do in the first place – pay for the maintenance, but not include the extra land and continue paying the rent we had agreed to until the end of the current contract.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There has been some speculation about the interiors at 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After this session, I will share with Members and the public some photos of the house before I moved in.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These photos were taken by my agent to point out some problem areas to SLA before the tenancy.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will also include current photos of the same places in the house for comparison.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second Minister Edwin Tong has explained the works that SLA normally does and did.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The photos have explanatory notes on the works done by SLA and the works done by me.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are indicative to give a sense of the state of the house and some of the works that were done.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not have a full set of photos on the original condition of the house.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Like other black and white bungalows, 26 Ridout Road required a fair amount of work.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is an old property and it had been unoccupied for more than four years.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I did work on the house to the extent that was allowed.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a conservation property, so there are limits on what you can do.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The money that I put in, I knew that I would not benefit from it after my lease is over.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It would all go back to the state.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is the deal when one rents a black and white, and I knew that.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Conflict of interest means I make a decision in a matter where I have an interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I took steps to deal with any perceived or potential conflict of interest.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: On my part, I told my agent everything had to be done strictly in accordance with the rules.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I spoke with the then-Senior Minister of State at MinLaw, Ms Indranee Rajah, and the then-Deputy Secretary at MinLaw.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I told them that I was looking at black and white bungalows.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I asked then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah whether, if any issue comes up to the Ministry, could she handle it.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I also said that if she needed to check anything, she could go to Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean and that I will tell Senior Minister Teo this.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I told Senior Minister Teo that I was looking at possibly renting a black and white bungalow and that if any issue comes up, SLA/MinLaw will check with then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah and, if she needed to, she will check with Senior Minister Teo.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I did that because Senior Minister Teo is senior to me.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I believe my agent so informed the SLA officers dealing with the lease.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I took these steps although rental issues do not come up to Ministers in the usual course.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Some people think that there is potential or perceived conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Actually, actual, potential or perceived conflict can only arise where I have an interest in the matter, I make a decision on the matter, then that will be actual conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I know that there are many important things that we have to deal with as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I did not enter public service to maximise my earnings, or try and pay less than I should, to the state.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean was consulted by Minister Shanmugam to step in to make decisions should the then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah need to escalate any matter.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We know that Senior Minister Teo was not called upon to make any decision at that time.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But given the above, I would like to ask whether it is appropriate for Senior Minister Teo to oversee an independent review of the matter.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The second point I would like to raise is this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The CPIB report states that Minister Shanmugam asked the then-Deputy Secretary of MinLaw for a list of properties available for the public to rent.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I would also like to ask if it was appropriate for Minister Shanmugam to ask for this list.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, with regard to myself, there is no conflict of interest for me to conduct the review.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am not involved in the rental transactions of both these properties.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I am not a party to the transactions, nor a participant, nor have I taken any actions or decisions regarding the rental of these two properties.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, I am not an involved party, I am not a subject of the CPIB investigation, nor, indeed, a subject of this Review either.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The investigations by the CPIB are independent, thorough and authoritative.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In my review, I have relied extensively on the CPIB's independent, thorough and authoritative report.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, Sir, I have no difficulty conducting this Review as an independent reviewer.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: On the subject of the Minister for Law having asked the Deputy Secretary for MinLaw, Sir, this point, actually, was noted by the CPIB in its investigation and was reported in the CPIB's findings.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, in fact, this point was looked into by CPIB.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Minister Shanmugam asked the Deputy Secretary for MinLaw for a list of properties that were available to the public for rent, and this was stated in the CPIB's report.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They are available via SLA's managing agents (MAs) responsible for marketing the properties on SLA's State Property Information Online (SPIO) system, prominently displayed with "For Lease" signs on the premises and available if a credible, potential tenant asks SLA or the MAs.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: SLA and MAs want to rent out these properties.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, they want people to know about them.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Hence, if a credible, prospective tenant were to ask SLA or the MAs which properties, for example, with certain characteristics that a credible, potential tenant has in mind, are available for lease, SLA or the MAs will provide the appropriate information, including on properties not listed on SPIO, but available for rent.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: SLA or MAs have received inquiries from ambassadors, company executives or professionals to rent state properties, and SLA provides the information to companies, too.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is, in fact, a 22-page slide deck, listing more than 10 properties of various types.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The listing includes the locations and characteristics of the properties so as to help the interested organisation or person to decide which property to rent.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And site visits could be arranged or would have been arranged.

speaker: The Senior Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, Sir, this is not unusual and it is not privileged information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may add on to that, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, because the question is: why did I ask the Deputy Secretary?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I know that they would give this information to credible, potential tenants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are a landlord, you have properties you want to rent, it is in your interest to give the information if you believe that the person is someone who is able to rent what you have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I could have asked SLA directly, and I know that SLA has given this information to others who will fall within the category of credible, prospective tenants: embassies and so on, companies, business persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think from SLA's perspective, I would be a credible, prospective tenant who is not going to run off without paying the rental.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I asked the Deputy Secretary, a senior Administrative Service officer, so that MinLaw knew and there was total transparency, instead of asking SLA directly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He would usually let the Permanent Secretary know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as senior Administrative Service officers, he and the Permanent Secretary will be able to go beyond me and report to the Head of Civil Service or the Prime Minister if they felt that anything needed to be brought up to that level – either the Deputy Secretary or the Permanent Secretary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I believed it was better to ask him rather than ask SLA directly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of the comments that have been made so far, I think, are made based on not realising that SLA will give these lists and has given these lists to others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they are secret, SLA cannot rent out these properties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once that is understood, then the question is: should I have asked SLA directly or through the Deputy Secretary?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have explained the reasons why I went through the Deputy Secretary.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first question pursues the second question raised by Mr Sitoh Yih Pin and, that is, with regard to good governance and Minister Shanmugam's decision to ask his Deputy Secretary, a very senior civil servant, for a list of properties for his personal occupation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fact is significant because, unlike Minister Vivian Balakrishnan's property, which was marketed through the SPIO portal amongst others, the information given to Minister Shanmugam for his personal use by the Deputy Secretary would appear to have been privileged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At minimum, the man on the street would not have equal access to this information and would have had to secure it at some cost.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, I would invite the Senior Minister to consider whether it would have been more appropriate for the Minister in question to have engaged an agent to inquire about properties that were available for rental.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should Singaporeans conclude that such actions by Ministers as instructing civil servants on personal matters and using official information for personal use is appropriate, above board and has been going on for a long time in the Public Service?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My second bucket of questions pertains to Reserves and land management, and I direct this at the Second Minister for Law.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Senior Minister explain if he probed into the substance of Minister Shanmugam's lack of confidence in a Public Service body under his charge?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The PAP routinely shuts down any proposal from the Opposition or the public that draws down or is perceived to draw down revenue from state land as "a raid on the Reserves".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: SLA increased the size of 26 Ridout Road with prime land by almost three times with no real impact on the cost of renting the property except for the usual maintenance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does this episode not highlight a need to close this policy loophole and put a value on vacant land which the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), anyway, would tax a Singaporean for?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And how many lessees have SLA negotiated with to enlarge their compounds as much as was enlarged for 26 Ridout Road?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are my questions for now, Deputy Speaker.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second Minister Edwin Tong has explained why, in the context of renting these properties, the GFA is of more significant importance than the total land area.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think Mr Pritam Singh would have heard the explanation and I am sure Second Minister Edwin Tong would be happy to repeat that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The reason is because when you buy a property, you want the land, and the land belongs to you for the entire duration, whether it is a 999-year lease or freehold or whatever it is or 99 years, and you can develop the property.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: When you rent the property for a short period of time, whether it is two years, three years, nine years, you cannot develop the property and you have to maintain it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think Second Minister Edwin Tong and Minister Shanmugam himself have explained it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The valuer values the land based on the valuer's professional judgement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am not one to second guess the professional judgement of a professional valuer.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The clearance of land is not unique to the case of 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I referred to that in my Statement earlier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The state property in Dalvey Estate had a significant amount of heavily vegetated land within the tenancy boundary.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In June 2018, the tenant of the property, as well as the neighbours living in nearby houses, raised persistent feedback on mosquitoes originating from this heavily vegetated area within the Dalvey Estate property, which was tenanted out.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: SLA's MA carried out fogging in the area.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In spite of this, this did not resolve the problem.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And with the agreement of the Dalvey Estate property's tenant, the fence line was, in fact, shifted inwards so that SLA could take over the maintenance of the vegetated area.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This case illustrates the issues at hand: that added land is not always a net gain in value and that some tenants may not be unhappy to reduce the land area to reduce the responsibility and the cost of maintenance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I hope that adequately addresses Mr Pritam Singh's question on that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On the issue of addressing why Minister Shanmugam asked the Deputy Secretary – and I think Mr Pritam Singh said this has been going on for a very long time – I think Mr Pritam Singh should not make general comments like that unless he can back them up.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I do not know because that was a comment that you made – that it has been going on for a very long time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I did not understand what you meant by that and if you do not recall having made that statement, I would appreciate it if you withdraw that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Minister Shanmugam explained why he approached the Deputy Secretary.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I have explained, this is not privileged information.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Any credible tenant, any credible prospective tenant – and there are many examples of that – who asks for this information, can either access it directly or can get it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There are other issues like how SLA manages state properties or, indeed, whether there are equity issues and so forth.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Perhaps, these associated issues, we can deal with them subsequently.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But let us satisfy ourselves first on these issues of corruption, abuse of power, conflict of interest, as several Members have asked.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Then, we can discuss the other associated issues.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Second Minister for Law, would you like to respond?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, I think Mr Pritam Singh said that the use of GFA as the main driver for rental and marketability of a property – and I think the Member used the word "loophole".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When you say "loophole", you suggest that it is a policy that has not been closed off, that for some reason, SLA chose to use GFA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think if Members heard my speech earlier, you will see that this is a market-driven consideration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We cannot set the policy and tell the valuers, just use GFA, ignore everything else, and expect that the market will adjust itself in a way which I have shown and I have explained.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I think the one real test of this is if you look at the Senior Minister's report – and I know you have it on the portal, I did not bring copies, you will recall an Annex.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I invite Members to pull it up from your portal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If you look at the table, the table says, "Rental rates of Black and Whites across Singapore".

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If Members heard my speech earlier, you will know that these black and white bungalows are managed by SLA as well as by external professional MAs – industry experts for real estate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I would add that more of SLA's Black and Whites are managed by external professional MAs than they are managed by SLA themselves and these MAs have their own independent, inhouse expert valuers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It has been vacant for almost five years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Senior Minister's report, he concluded that Mr Shanmugam had declared the potential conflict of interest and removed himself from the chain of command.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, how should these standards be looked at in the light of Minister Shanmugam's case?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second supplementary question is a short one for Minister Shanmugam on his CPIB interview.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Deputy Speaker, I am conscious that I am surrounded by lawyers and I am not one myself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I will try and explain on this issue of conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On conflict of interest, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim has referenced the Code of Conduct and asked essentially whether there is potential or perceived conflict of interest in the case.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Conflict of interest arises when two things coincide: when a person's duty, for example, a function or responsibility from the office or position that he occupies, conflicts with his own personal interests.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, both of these elements have to exist.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If there is one without the other, no conflict arises.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A conflict can be actual, which arises when a person, in fact, makes a decision on a matter where his duty and his personal interests in that matter remain.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, his duty and his personal interests are there and he made a decision in his capacity which affects his personal interests.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Or it can be a potential conflict of interest, which arises when a conflicted person is in a position to but does not yet make such a decision.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is a potential conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Either of these scenarios has to depend on the specific facts of each case.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A conflict is not a conflict just because of someone's perception of the facts.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He informed MinLaw to clear any matter related to the tenancy, if it arose, with then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah and, if necessary, with myself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: By removing himself from the chain of command, Minister Shanmugam took himself out of any decision-making responsibility in the matter.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, he no longer had any duty in this matter and, therefore, that factor disappears.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Once there is a recusal, no duty arises.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I am told by lawyers that the best way of dealing with any potential conflict of interest is to disclose the potential conflict and then proceed to recuse oneself altogether from the decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this is what happened here on the facts of this case.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, when we talk about perception of conflict, once we are clear that potential conflict no longer exists and we know that actual conflict did not exist, that should dispel the idea that there is a perception of conflict of interest in the minds of any fair-minded person.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Shanmugam, would you like to respond to Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Deputy Speaker, just two clarifications for Second Minister for Law Mr Edwin Tong.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have a clarification to put to the Senior Minister.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The financial sector and banks have a category called "politically exposed persons" (PEP).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Depending on jurisdiction, it can include Ministers, Members of Parliament, leaders of political parties of any persuasion and their immediate family members.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Should the Public Service consider having a framework whereby the personal transactions of PEPs with Government agencies be automatically flagged out for additional scrutiny?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This helps further ensure that public officers are in the clear, protects the public officers from allegations of malfeasance and it also helps ensure that a PEP is in the clear as well, regardless of their political persuasion.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have a lot of difficulty opening a bank account in another country.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Banking transactions can involve – and this is the reason – the transfer of substantial funds that flow rapidly – and many times even in a day or in an hour – across borders from multiple sources to multiple destinations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The banks are, therefore, required to "KYC", that is, know their customers, and exercise vigilance to flag suspicious transactions so as to prevent money laundering and terrorism financing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Those are the two principal reasons why the PEP framework has been established for financial institutions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The considerations, Sir, are different for transactions by political officeholders and public officers with Public Service agencies.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A potential conflict of interest can arise in a transaction with a Government agency, and also in making a policy or an administrative decision.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there may have been no transaction, but a public officer or a political officeholder may be making a policy which impacts him.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Or in a transaction by persons in political office or in the Civil Service with non-public sector organisations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And given the context of the work of public agencies, a number of measures have already been put in place.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For public sector transactions, there are suitability checks carried out on the counterparty and, even in this case, for the rental of state properties, there were suitability checks carried out on the prospective tenant.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Public Service also has an internal disclosure policy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, he is required to report any wrongful practice that he comes across.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There will be an investigation into the allegations in what we conventionally call the "whistleblower", and he will be protected if he has made the report in good faith.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there are multiple measures in place, and it is quite different from the very rapid transactions that can take place, the transfer of funds in a bank, and that is why the banks require a PEP-type of system upfront.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, even if checks and processes by the public sector organisation do not flag a conflict of interest, the individual still remains responsible and will be held accountable if he is subsequently found to have a conflict of interest, abused his powers or improperly made use of privileged information.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Public Service will continue to reference the best practices in other sectors, such as the financial sector, to keep improving its system of governance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, once a year, officers in positions of authority over funds and so forth have to take leave and somebody else takes his place.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, the public sector has rules where persons in such financially sensitive positions cannot stay in that position sort of indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But these are examples which add to the guidelines.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But the general principle still applies all the time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, I have a clarification for Senior Minister Teo on the standards expected of our Ministers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, does he agree with me that actually the Code of Conduct embodies the highest standards expected of our Ministers in the conduct of their public affairs and it should not be the subject of legal arguments or technicalities?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I explained to another lawyer earlier, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim, what conflict of interest means.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Two things must come together at the same time, and this is not a legal description.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It also underpins what our understanding of conflict of interest is in the Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There must be some official power that you have over some matter and that matter coincides with a personal interest of that person.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is an actual conflict of interest if the person with that duty, with those powers, uses them on a matter in which he has a personal interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is a potential conflict of interest if that person retains that power and there is a matter which is there, which is his personal interest, but no decision or action has yet been taken by that person.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The potential conflict of interest is removed if the person removes himself from that duty.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Ms Sylvia Lim is a lawyer and I think she understands that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is very important and I explained that earlier, and I hope that that will satisfy Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But once the actual conflict of interest and the potential conflict of interest have been removed, that should dispel the perception of conflict of interest in any fair-minded person.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My first supplementary question is really on the determination that the conduct of the Ministers in this case is consistent with the Ministerial Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why was that determination not passed to an independent third party to make, for example, the Auditor-General's Office (AGO) or an independent judge?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not asserting that Senior Minister Teo's review is not independent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the perception that that judgement, that determination, was being made by someone who is not a senior colleague of the Ministers concerned but is an independent entity would go some way to address some of these public concerns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And the Auditor-General does have expertise in understanding norms of best practice within the Public Service, norms of corporate governance, audit compliance and so on and so forth and, I would note, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, that in reply to a Parliamentary Question I filed, there had been two occasions when the Auditor-General was asked to do a special audit in the last 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The first occasion was to interrogate the claims made by an Opposition leader, Mr Chee Soon Juan, in the 1990s; the second occasion was to investigate the finances of Aljunied-Hougang Town Council.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, why could the Auditor-General not have been called in to make that determination, not of corruption – I appreciate the work of the CPIB, and the CPIB's expertise is prevention of corruption act – but to make a determination about consistency with the Ministerial Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, I want to come back to para 40 of the Report, on Minister Shanmugam requesting the information about some of the black and white bungalows from the Deputy Secretary at MinLaw.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am trying to understand how this is not problematic because, based on the Report, SLA has explained that there is a deliberate policy intent here that, in certain times, like in a down market cycle, the deliberate intent is not to make too transparent all these listings, which is why 26 Ridout Road was not listed on the SPIO.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is not by accident, if I can just read very briefly from The Straits Times article that talks about why SLA has this policy: "When market conditions are poor and supply exceeds demand, or the occupancy rates for specific estates are low, 'publishing complete listings of all vacant properties online would result in these properties visibly competing for the limited demand, and thus may not help the landlord maximise outcomes'".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, in this case, how is the action of the Minister for Law to ask for information on properties – some of which are not listed on the SPIO into one, simple, consolidated factsheet – how is that not problematic?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, on the methodology, to choose a methodology of direct tenancy negotiation versus open bidding, I understand from Second Minister Edwin Tong's Statement earlier that, in a direct tenancy —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, perhaps you can take that later, because we want to clear the more fundamental issues first.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I did not want to bring up that history and link the two.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But since the Member has, I may have some comments on that as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Why not the Auditor-General and why the CPIB?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Was there a loss of funds because somebody was not doing the accounts properly and so on?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think, eventually, the Government, the Prime Minister, has to take responsibility for that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And we know the reputation of the CPIB.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is a very thorough, it is a very independent agency and, as I said just now, it can be quite a fearsome agency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And the fact that the Prime Minister called in the CPIB to carry out this investigation on two senior Ministers shows the seriousness with which this Government and the Prime Minister took this issue.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I suppose, Mr Speaker, Sir, if we had called in the Auditor-General, Mr Leon Perera would have been standing up, asking me why did you not call in the CPIB, since the CPIB is the most appropriate agency to investigate such an issue.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This idea that there is some secret list somewhere which nobody knows about, and that renting such properties confers some benefit or privilege which others cannot access.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think the investigation – and what I have stated and what Second Minister Edwin Tong has stated – refutes both of these; dispels both of these.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is public information what properties are available for lease.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: SLA wants to maximise the renting out of these properties and to do its best for the state in doing so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there is no reason for SLA not to want to provide those properties and the list of those properties.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Pritam Singh earlier talked about individuals having to go to considerable expense to find out and so on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In the case of the company that I talked about, they did not have to pay anybody to get the list.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They asked SLA, and SLA was quite happy to give it to them without charging them because SLA wants to rent out its properties.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It may not be on SPIO, but any credible tenant who wants to rent those properties will know which properties are available.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, let us dispel these two things and put them to rest, although Mr Leon Perera does bring them up.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I thank him so that I can explain these things quite clearly.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think I have addressed Mr Leon Perera's points.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding the findings that both Ministers were cleared of any wrongdoing, the revelations of the Report have since raised more concerns from the public.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, the first question is for Second Minister Edwin Tong.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: My second question is for Minister Shanmugam and Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Ministers' Code of Conduct clearly mandates that a Minister must scrupulously avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest between their official duties and private financial interests.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: So, it is in the interest of transparency that both Ministers declare all their property assets.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If there are any, will the two Ministers declare if these properties have been rented out anytime during the lease of 26 and 31 Ridout Road to assure the public that there are no monetary gains from lease arbitration?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I did mention what the Code of Conduct does say and what it covers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I will leave the rest of the questions to Second Minister Edwin Tong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, at any point in time up till the time when it is off the market, that is, when a tenant confirms his tenancy, it continues to be marketed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, to answer the Member's question whether before, during or even after, as long as the incoming tenant has not confirmed, it remains on the market and it will be marketed by the agents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Senior Minister Teo stated that he was not within the chain of command in making the decision, therefore, he was not involved in the matter and, therefore, he headed this review.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Senior Minister Teo also mentioned earlier that he relied on the independent CPIB report.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, when the declaration was made to him back then, and Senior Minister Teo was made aware of this matter, I assumed that he was already satisfied then that all actual or potential conflicts of interest were satisfactorily addressed back then and, therefore, the matter was put to rest at the time; otherwise, he would have voiced his concerns at that time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given the public interest in the matter and the importance of public perception that there was no wrongdoing, what was the reasoning behind asking Senior Minister Teo to investigate the matter this round?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Were there really no other options or individuals who could have led the review?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, CPIB usually looks at whether there have been any breaches of criminal laws, which they have investigated here and cleared the Ministers of doing.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The review headed by Senior Minister Teo would also need to go beyond criminal matters, including looking at whether there have been any breaches of the Ministerial code of conduct or the rules of prudence and also about the perception and the conflicts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I ask again because if Senior Minister Teo had been satisfied back then that any actual or potential conflicts of interests were actually addressed satisfactorily, it seems strange to ask him to now relook his earlier conclusion that everything was adequately addressed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, apart from relying on the CPIB report and given the questions raised, they actually go beyond criminal matters, were there any other specific steps that were taken to ensure that there was adequate independence throughout the review?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As I explained, Mr Deputy Speaker, this is similar if you had a situation where you have a Chairman of a company or an organisation, and a director comes to him and says "I have a conflict of interest, I am declaring it, and I am taking steps to make sure the conflict of interest does not arise".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is the situation that I am in.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is very different if you had an organisation which convenes a disciplinary committee and the persons who convene the disciplinary committee take part in the disciplinary committee themselves and are involved parties.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think one must differentiate between the two situations, and I hope that Ms He Ting Ru is able to do that.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I am seeking a clarification from the Senior Minister.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I know the Senior Minister has explained to the other Members on their queries.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I will come back to this point on Minister Shanmugam asking the Deputy Secretary for a list of the property and I have been trying to understand the Senior Minister's explanation and I find that there are still issues that we need to overcome here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And because we are talking about a Minister who is asking a Deputy Secretary in his Ministry a question relating to his private interests, not in the course of his work, and then, on the part of the Deputy Secretary, I think there is an issue whether the Deputy Secretary had to decide whether this is a matter of work.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And if it is a matter of work within his responsibility, is it contingent on him to answer?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Is it appropriate for him to answer this question?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do not think these issues have been adequately clarified.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is important to clarify this as a matter of guidance for the Civil Service, because the civil servant, the senior civil servants must know where the line is drawn.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For example, Senior Minister, on this issue, the Deputy Secretary could have politely informed Minister Shanmugam that he can get his agent to direct a question to SLA.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: That I think would, in my view, be an appropriate form of answer rather than to take it upon himself.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, I would like to ask the Senior Minister to reconsider his earlier answers in light of the issues I have raised because it pertains to – I think it is important for the future when a senior civil servant or a civil servant has to answer a question from an officeholder – what he is entitled to do, what he should do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And Minister Shanmugam explained, in his own terms, why he decided to approach the Deputy Secretary because he was doing this in an open, transparent way to tell his Ministry, "I am doing this.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is no secret about it." He could have got an agent and go and approach SLA and then later on, SLA discovers that actually the Minister was behind it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In this case, I think the Minister told his Ministry and was quite open and transparent about it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And if he had got an agent to go and approach SLA, and then SLA provides information or whatever it is and, in the end, they discovered that actually the person behind it was the Minister and the Minister did not say anything about it, the question is whether that is better or worse?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But in this case, it was done openly and transparently, so I think that is important.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, as I said, was there privileged information that was asked for?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think those are the principal issues at hand.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: We are still on the "conflict of interest" theme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In specific answer to Mr Dennis Tan, Senior Minister Teo answered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I explained in some detail why specifically the Deputy Secretary, and the Member heard the Senior Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What was in my mind is, I should let MinLaw know because, that way, the Permanent Secretary will know, the Deputy Secretary will know.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I could have written direct to SLA or I could have asked my agent to write direct to SLA; and I know based, on practice, they do give this information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I explained why I thought that it was better to ask the Deputy Secretary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was better to ask the Deputy Secretary rather than going direct to SLA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I had gone direct to SLA and SLA receives a letter, is that better?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or is it better that there is the Deputy Secretary who, together with the Permanent Secretary, knows that this is happening, gets a list, and I look at it and then I recuse myself if I want to proceed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think it was important for me to have told my Ministry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is not on a private errand or something.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I looked at it as I am telling my Ministry and saying – I mean I did not express it – but that is the understanding; they understood me and I understood my thinking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is, if I ask you, you get it, I look at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That way, the Ministry knows what I am doing, rather than writing directly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I see that as something that is entirely proper.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think that is open to serious misinterpretation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: What I meant was, it is important to observe the spirit and not just the letter of the Code.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I think if you look at the context of what I was saying, you will appreciate the context because there are many examples that are given.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: You may just follow the examples, but if you do not follow the spirit, that is not good enough.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, you must follow the letter of the Code, but that is not good enough.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I thought I should clarify that, in case it is taken out of context.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And does he think that other Ministers should do the same in future when faced with a similar situation as Minister Shanmugam?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, can I have Mr Giam's question again, please?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Because we discussed earlier that he could have asked SLA through an agent, but he chose not to.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: He chose to go to his Deputy Secretary instead.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Why could he not go to his agent, get his agent to ask SLA a question and then inform his Permanent Secretary separately?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And did he make clear to his Deputy Secretary at the time that he was asking him, that he was asking for the purpose of transparency?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I thought I have explained this a number of times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as I said to Mr Dennis Tan, is that better?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or is it better to ask a much more senior officer and let him know?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, everybody understood – yes, this is why I am asking him, he will keep the Permanent Secretary informed, and he will get me a list and then we see how we will proceed, rather than going direct to SLA.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I will take the three hands on this theme and then also open the floor to the other theme, which Mr Xie Yao Quan had raised, which Second Minister Edwin Tong would like to respond to.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And also, I think, Mr Leon Perera had a third supplementary question to Second Minister Edwin Tong.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, the three hands are Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Mr Leong Mun Wai and then Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And then, we will go on to a different theme.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, if I could ask the three Members to stay on theme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, Mr Deputy Speaker, I would like to hear directly from the two Ministers, Mr Shanmugam and Dr Balakrishnan, if on hindsight, whether there are specific actions that they undertook that they now believe, at the very least, could be perceived as a conflict of interest, keeping in mind that we operate as public servants and perceptions are very important for public figures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And especially since the Ministerial Code of Conduct, of course, includes this more stringent qualification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I have a second question but I will leave it for a subsequent theme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is an important question, and it is at the heart of a lot of misunderstandings, even from lawyers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From what I hear from the Members, there was no potential conflict either because I recused myself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members agree, from what they are saying, that there was no potential conflict, they accept the conclusions of the report on that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And let me explain what is at the heart of the confusion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you talk about conflict, what are you talking about?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is an interest on one side and there is a duty on the other side.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If one of those does not exist, there is no conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not matter that you took no part in it, it does not matter that you recused yourself, it does not matter that the matter was decided perfectly properly, as long as a member of the public or anyone else can take the view that you are in perceived conflict, you are in conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot run any government on that basis.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister for Health goes to a hospital for a knee replacement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He goes to a hospital for a knee replacement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is not in actual conflict, he is not asking them to charge him anything less; otherwise, Prime Minister will ask CPIB to look at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He is not bringing forward his surgery ahead of others against medical advice.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But someone can say, "You are the Minister for Health.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have a say in appointing the CEOs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are the person who decides on the structure and, in some ways, their career progress.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They might treat you better than they might treat others.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And therefore, you are in perceived conflict." Can a government work on this basis?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That it is entirely up to a subjective viewpoint on perception, perceived conflict?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or the Minister for Home Affairs, in a personal capacity, goes to file a Police report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can someone say, "Well, that creates a perceived conflict of interest because you are in charge ultimately of the Police Force and they might, therefore, handle the investigations differently.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And therefore, that is a perception of conflict." In anything dealing with that report, the Minister must recuse himself, he must have no part to play, he must treat himself as a private citizen and the matter must be handled by others appropriate within the Police and the Ministry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can give you a string of examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister for Education, his son applies to a school which has some discretion whether to admit children or not.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is he in a perceived conflict of interest?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason why we are ranked as highly as we are and the reason why this Government is not corrupt is because we take these things seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has got to have commonsense, it has got to be the spirit, it has got to be the letter, and it has got to be applied sensibly and properly, but rigorously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rather than just repeating the word, what is the perceived conflict?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That, in essence, is what is being said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If that is so, that is a new principle, because some people may perceive you to be in conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is not the principle in the Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is my answer to Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Oh, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, do you have a clarification?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The clarification is that, for Minister Shanmugam, on hindsight, there are no perceived conflicts of interest in his mind that he would have otherwise corrected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sorry, Sir, I missed part of Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, maybe if the Member can repeat it again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Yes, it is that, in the Minister's mind, there are indeed no perceived conflicts of interest, on hindsight, that you would otherwise have alternatively acted in a different way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that was very much in my mind, which is why I went and took the step.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way this Government operates, Senior Minister Teo, previously in charge of the Civil Service, knows all about how our rules operate, and that is why I went to him and said, if this comes up, can the then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah come to you?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, I could have left it with then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah could have dealt with it herself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, yes, the answer is yes, it was in my mind, which is why I took the steps that I took.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two questions, both for the Senior Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before that, what I would like to say is that I think what we are discussing today is that most of us believe in the integrity of our Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But what we are trying to establish is: are there conflicted situations that we should avoid, going forward?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then, from this, if we agree that there are some conflicted situations, whether the outcome of the terms and conditions of the contract reflect that, or whether the terms and conditions reflect a conflicted situation or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are still in the process of discussing and debating.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope the Senior Minister will be patient that we probably cannot conclude whether there is a conflicted situation or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But first of all, now, we are talking about whether there is a conflicted situation or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I have two questions I would like to ask.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, the Senior Minister himself said if someone has the power over his personal interest, then it may potentially be a conflicted situation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister for Law has explained that it may not be a conflicted situation, although the CEO of SLA reports directly to him.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question is with regard to the Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think the Senior Minister mentioned just now that it should not just be the letter of the Code of Conduct but also the spirit.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we expect our Government to be a government of integrity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do you not think that our expectations and the expectations of many Singaporeans would be that you do not touch anything that you are doubtful?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can I ask the Senior Minister, under the current situation, does he not think the two Ministers should have considered the possibility of negative public perception?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As for the perceived conflict of interest, as I explained earlier, if one has dealt with it, that there is no actual conflict of interest, there is no potential conflict of interest, then that should be sufficient to dispel the idea of a perceived conflict of interest in any fair-minded person.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The fact that, yes, he has some power over the appointment of, whether he assesses that the CEO of SLA performed well or not, that will always be there.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: You cannot remove that, but that will mean that the Prime Minister, for example, cannot do anything, because he has powers over practically every agency in Singapore!

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think one has to look at the realities of the situation, what steps people have taken and, most importantly, to have confidence in the integrity of the Public Service and our public officers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think, in this case, our public officers showed a very high degree of integrity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, when the MA asked SLA is there some VVIP track, the SLA officer replied emphatically to the MA – no, there is no such thing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Every potential tenant or tenant has to be treated equally.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is a testament to the quality of the public officers that we have.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They know what integrity means and they stand by it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And so, I think we have to give credit to our public officers, that they know how to behave and they know what to do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is a very important aspect of integrity of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On the Code of Conduct, I would, first, like to dispel another misconception which Mr Leong's question perhaps inadvertently perpetuates – that these are relatively cheap bungalows.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And you can see the facts for yourself that it is not true, and I hope that you will help to spread the word that it is not true.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The bungalows are rented out at market rates.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The agents out there have a pretty good idea what they are worth.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think we should dispel this idea completely, which I think Mr Leong Mun Wai must have inadvertently contributed to through his question, that these bungalows are going at a relatively cheap rate.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think also that Second Minister Edwin Tong has explained why the expenditure is required to set these properties, to make them habitable and rentable.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am not a property person myself, but I do some simple arithmetic.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If you have a property which is not tenanted, not in good condition and cannot be rented out, you get no rent from it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But you have to put money in to cut the grass, to make sure the building, at least, remains in some decent condition, it does not fall down and so on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is a complete loss to SLA, if it does not put the property in a condition which is rentable.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But many of the things that they do will last for quite a long time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, if the water tank is very poor condition, you replace the water tank, it will last you 10 years, at least.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If you have a problem with the roof and the roof is leaking, when you replace it, do major repairs on it, it will last you at least 10 years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If you have problems with the beams and the structures because there is a lot of wood in there and you do work on it, it will last you maybe 10 years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is amortised over a period of time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: SLA does its cost-benefit analysis to see whether it is worthwhile.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, if a tenant is prepared to pay, let us say, in round numbers, $20,000 in rent, $25,000 in rent, $20,000 in rent in the first year will bring back $240,000, $25,000 will bring back $300,000.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: After that, what they have done is still good for another six to seven years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, if you have a tenant who is prepared to rent it from you for 3+3 or 3+2+2, and is reliable, prepared to give you good rental, it is a worthwhile thing to do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Otherwise, SLA will have to put in money every year to maintain the land, to cut the grass, to make sure there are no mosquitoes, to make sure that this conserved property does not fall down and collapse.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Whereas by putting in that investment, they can get a return on investment over a number of years, which will then bring benefits to the state.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These are the kinds of tradeoffs, cost-benefit analysis that SLA does, which I think the SLA officers do know and are cognisant that they need to do things which are value-for-money, good cost-benefit analysis and bring benefit to the state.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think our public officers do have integrity and they do look after the interests of the state and all of us.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
