speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Pritam Singh, the question that you want to ask previously?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A number of Members have come forward and asked questions since the first questions I asked.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The fact of the matter here is that I do not believe anybody is making an allegation that the Minister is corrupt, somebody is corrupt in the system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The issue I think we are having to deal with here is the Ministerial Code of Conduct and a specific course of action that was taken by the Minister when he instructed his Deputy Secretary to get some information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I will just share the problem with that, just over the course of the last two hours.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Senior Minister Teo says it is not a secret list.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Minister Shanmugam is a little bit more qualified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He says, "Credible people will get that information." So, within that, we can see some differentiation of why to seek that information could be conceived, by some people, at least, including myself, as actually seeking information, which probably, out of a matter of prudence, would be better sought by an agent appointed by the Minister – which was the question Senior Minister did not answer in my first round of questions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Would it have been better, in his perspective as the Minister reviewing this episode, for Minister Shanmugam to appoint an agent and he would still have been able to make the necessary declarations, vis-à-vis conflict with a senior civil servant and so forth?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It would appear from SLA policy that the fact that the Valuer did not know who was the person that was ultimately going to rent the property, suggests that this would not have been so much of a problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I think we have not interrogated that and how the system can be improved if a situation like this comes up again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In my view, it is much more prudent, in view of the Ministerial Code of Conduct, which is onerous, to keep your official matters and your personal matters separate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There is no need to ask a senior civil servant this information when you know you can get an agent to secure the same information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not sure whether the Senior Minister can agree with that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second point I would like to raise is that Minister Shanmugam spoke of an innuendo that when we ask questions about rental and the land area being increased, that, somehow, this is a personal attack against him.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My point when I raised my first set of questions was: there is a question of political optics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: When we want to rent, let us say, a landed property, an intermediate terrace house would cost less than a corner terrace or semi-detached house.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If you are a pet lover, you can clearly see that connection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If you have a big family like Minister Vivian Balakrishnan, that additional land has utility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Hence, in the minds of people, the view is, surely, there ought to be some value attached to that, notwithstanding the clarification Second Minister for Law made about how the Valuers in SLA look at it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that is the public perception that has raised some of these questions that have come to bear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I just have a final point which was triggered by what Member Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim asked.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: He asked about the process of the CPIB investigation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That is my take because that is the same conclusion that I come to, and we are at one, Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The issue now is one of perception of conduct, of conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, we agree there is no corruption, abuse of power, personal benefit and so on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The issue now is one of conflict of interest, actual conflict of interest, potential conflict of interest, perceived conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And we have gone through this a number of times.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Before I go any further, again, if I said "anybody" can get the list, this is in the context of "anybody" who is a credible potential tenant.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And that is clearly the context in which I made that comment.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, there is no air gap between what Mr Shanmugam said with regard to credible tenants and what I said.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On perceptions, conflict of interest, I can only repeat what I said earlier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There must be a duty coming from the position which the person holds which impacts upon the second factor, which is a private interest of that person.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If those two come together, then there is a potential conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think that is what a fair-minded person will come to.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Those are the points that I want to make.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think I will stop there and let Second Minister Edwin Tong respond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On questions and innuendos, I want to make it very clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said in my Ministerial Statement earlier, I welcome questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is important that we discuss this robustly, thoroughly, fully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is how we keep the integrity in the system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not run away from any of the questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, I wanted a full in-depth investigation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point about innuendos, I mean, we can go through the different questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are prepared to come up and have ourselves be questioned, to answer, explain, let Singaporeans judge for themselves what did we do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Leader of the Opposition has talked about optics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think, if necessary, we will talk about the optics, too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want to answer all the questions and I fear no questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I was quite careful to say it is not just SLA's valuers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is a view that is taken of the market, and we have to be guided by the market, market forces in how we look at this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When we say that it is the GFA that is the main factor that determines the price and the marketability, it is not just an SLA or a policy position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is that taken by the industry, by the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I pointed Members to the Annex in Senior Minister Teo's report because that represents all the Black and Whites in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are not told by SLA what the guide rent should be or how to determine it, but they go back to market forces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, this is a factor that is looked at and it has to be looked at in the context of what are the right market forces to it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I mentioned, too, in my speech, that each of these MAs, their arrangement with SLA incentivises them to maximise occupancy and drive rental.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, there is no incentive for them to try to assess a guide rent otherwise than by market forces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I hope that puts this matter to rest because it is not that GFA is the only factor, neither did I say that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Location, condition and all these are factors that I think I mentioned.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the main factor, when it comes to a black and white heritage property, is really the GFA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: For Second Minister Edwin Tong, firstly, the methodology of direct negotiated rental versus open bidding system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second one is really I am just trying to reconcile what has been said in the report about how certain properties, black and white bungalows are not listed in the SPIO in a down cycle, because you do not want too much transparency which may deter bidders, they can see a lot of vacant properties – and I quoted something from The Straits Times earlier about that policy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We do not outsource it to someone else.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We believe we should take responsibility for the Code of Conduct and the conduct of our Ministers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To Mr Leon Perera's first question on market conditions, the market conditions are set out in, well, first, Members can see the table that I circulated earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I think that answers the Member's first question.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the Member's second question, he said that the Black and Whites were not put on SPIO because "we do not want too much transparency".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would say, please do not put words in my mouth, or put it in my speech.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Going back to first principles, SLA is the landlord and I told Members in my speech that we want to maximise occupancy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What is the best way in which they can be rented?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In an up market, you want to make sure that it is as exposed as possible because there is more demand than there is supply.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a down market, it is the contrary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But not for lack of transparency reasons, as the Member tries to suggest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is because you do not want to have yourselves have each property bid against itself, to have more supply than demand exhibited on all the portals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, what is being done in those situations is for some properties, at the discretion of the MAs, to be listed on SPIO.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Other properties might well find their way on other property portals like Property Guru and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The MA and each of their real estate agents in their network would, in fact, have the full list of all the assets that are available for renting.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is to ensure that the right strategy is adopted to ensure that we market it in the right way that coheres with the dynamics and movements of the market at the relevant time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The first is to hon Senior Minister Teo.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the fact that he was installed as the head of the chain of command in relation to the dealings pertaining to 26 Ridout Road, now that we have established the facts, if you were to turn the clock back, are there any facts that you would have expected to be raised to your attention?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not seeking an elaborate answer, a brief answer on that would suffice.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My next question is to the hon Minister Shanmugam.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the sheer size of the property at 26 Ridout Road, there have been some comments in the public about whether Ministers living in such private properties have a connection with the people and would be able to relate to the people, and also whether such acts engender a picture of inequality in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder whether the hon Minister has a response to that.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Yes, we can go past 5.30 pm if needed.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Not for your response, I mean for this debate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It might take a fair bit of time, but anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many Singaporeans face challenges in today's economic climate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, inequality is one of the biggest issues we are grappling with not just here in Singapore, but the world over.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How we deal with it and the values that inform our approach are important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I often speak about inequality when I speak outside to audiences because it is a critical issue for Singapore and also because it is seared into me, because I have gone through it myself, seen it first-hand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is not just an academic exercise for me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I stayed in Bukit Ho Swee as a young boy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, as a teenager, I lived in a 3-room flat in Block 3 Ghim Moh.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: About 20 years later, as a senior counsel, I owned a GCB in Astrid Hill and, prior to that, I owned a house in Oei Tiong Ham Park, also very nearby, though I never lived in that house.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The distance between Block 3 Ghim Moh and Astrid is only about one kilometre.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the psychological and financial distance within Ghim Moh and Astrid or Oei Tiong Ham is oceans-wide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As an undergraduate, when I lived in Ghim Moh, I used to cross the old Bukit Timah Railway Line, walk up East Essex Lane to the bus stop along Holland Road, to take a bus to Law School.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Twenty years later, I would drive along Holland Road.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same bus stop, instead of walking up the left, I made a right turn into Coronation Road West to go into Queen Astrid Park, to go to my house there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think a lot about inequality and the gap, not least because I have straddled the gap and have lived at both extremes – rental and GCB.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, for my part, the circumstances that I grew up with are seared into me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And when you have gone through the experiences I have, you will never forget them, regardless of how successful you become.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not deal with inequality by preventing poor kids from doing well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee Kuan Yew set up a system that allowed a poor Indian kid to become a successful lawyer, to do well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You tackle inequality by providing for social mobility, by helping people to move up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do this, for example, by providing good support, opportunities, help everyone to move up and redistributing income from those who have succeeded to the poor or less well-off through taxes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can tax the rich more and redistribute while making sure to keep the system fair.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you tax too much, the wealthy will leave.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to make sure that those who are less well-off are properly taken care of and there are social mobility and opportunity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A famous American jurist, Oliver Wendell Holmes, once said, "Taxes are the price we pay for civilization".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In my case, all I have, I got from Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is only right for me to give back.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dealing with inequality is always a work-in-progress and how can we continue to find ways to bring about greater equality?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We must encourage those who have more, who have achieved more, to come forward and contribute their time and talent and resources to help make a stronger society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need people to step forward, help fellow Singaporeans, including in Public Service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if you look at Mr Lee's approach, since the start, he brought in people who were doing well outside and those who had the heart to serve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some were independently very wealthy, but he persuaded them to give up their careers in the private sector to come in to serve Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They, together with Mr Lee, did more than most to make Singapore a more equal society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether you should serve or not should depend on your heart: do you want to help serve, make lives of Singaporeans better?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee brought in people as Ministers and Members of Parliament regardless of their background and it did not matter if they were rich or poor, from trade unionists like Mr Mahmud Awang from the Singapore Traction Company Employees Union, Mr Ho See Beng from the Printers Union, to highly successful businessmen and professionals, like Mr Lim Kim San and Mr E W Barker.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, Mr Lim Kim San, he was a shrewd successful businessman when Mr Lee brought him into Public Service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee said he helped change the fortunes of Singapore as HDB Chairman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He then served as Minister in various Ministries, including Finance, Defence, National Development where he was also responsible for building HDB flats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He lived in a very large bungalow at Dalvey Road.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr EW Barker was the Minister who drafted the Separation Agreement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Should Mr Lee have said to him, "Eddie, you're a successful lawyer living in Queen Astrid Park.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Goh Keng Swee stayed in a very large black and white bungalow at Goodwood Hill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was Deputy Prime Minister, key architect of modern Singapore – economy, defence, education, across the board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Hon Sui Sen served as Finance Minister; Chairman, Economic Development Board (EDB), President of the Development Bank of Singapore (DBS).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also rented a black and white at Malcolm Road.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or I should add, at that time, it was among the benefits that senior officials could rent houses reserved for them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But they remain the same type of black and white houses that Minister Vivian Balakrishnan and I are staying in, not any more prestigious or less prestigious then or now, and some, of course, quite rundown, as compared to modern GCBs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it becomes a matter of personal preference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should add that I am not in any way seeking to compare myself or other current Ministers with the Ministers I have mentioned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not believe the homes I lived in have affected my ability to serve and empathise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was doing well in my career as a lawyer while I was serving as a backbench Member of Parliament for more than 20 years before I became a Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I became a Member of Parliament in September 1988 when I was 29.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At that time, I was a few months away from becoming a partner.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I knew it would be very challenging to manage my career and be a Member of Parliament at the same time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I agreed to stand for elections in 1988, become a Member of Parliament and do what I can to make Singapore a better place.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Every hardworking Member of Parliament will know that the requirements of being a Member of Parliament in terms of time, energy are considerable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From the beginning of my journey as a Member of Parliament, I found it demanding but I also found it inspiring.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Demanding because my legal career required my full attention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it was inspiring because I was doing what I could to forge a community in Chong Pang.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I drew meaning and purpose from serving my residents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I came into politics in 1988, most Chong Pang residents were generally less well-off.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many were like my parents, who had to work tirelessly to provide the best for their children.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They want their children to do better, and I want to be there to help them to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, although it was challenging to juggle between being a Member of Parliament and my legal career, I carried on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, in 2008, I was asked by the Prime Minister to become a Minister because Prof Jayakumar who had been Minister for Law for 20 years by then, was stepping down.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I was 48, at the peak of my career.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would have been much easier for me to continue being a full-time lawyer than to join Cabinet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did also seriously think about the cutback in income.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had to assess what it would mean for me, my family, and assess that against what I could contribute by serving Singaporeans as a Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I asked myself, "on my last day on earth" – this is a question I ask frequently when I reflect back on my life – what would I have wanted to have done with my life?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or also spend some time doing some good work for the community and others and perhaps some good for the country?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many things that people spend time on will not seem worthwhile to have done in the rear-view mirror when your life is about to end.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, having twice or three times more money would not make me twice or three times happier or fulfilled.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I accepted the Prime Minister's invitation, agreed to enter full-time politics as a Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was and continues to be an honour and a privilege to serve Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, all I have, I got from Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was Singapore's system, the system that Mr Lee Kuan Yew and Dr Goh Keng Swee and their team set up to provide stability, good standards of living, good schools and opportunities that allowed me and so many others to achieve what we have, despite where we started, and in spite of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I was fortunate to have been born in Singapore and I want to help make policies to make sure other Singaporeans have the opportunities that I did.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not suggesting that I made a special sacrifice in taking a pay cut or moving from my family home.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have spent more than half my life in Parliament and more than half my life with Chong Pang.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not hide what I earned as a lawyer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My empathy did not increasingly decrease as my houses got larger, or as I made more money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Over the years, no one raised any issue of my empathy or my ability to serve, in the 10 years I was living in my GCB at Astrid Hill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does it get more affected when you move from a GCB that you own to a Black and White that you rent?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is that the way we are going to judge politicians?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I hope Members will seek to make Singaporeans and everyone understand what is involved because we should not start judging people on the basis of where they live or how successful they were in the private sector and then say, "You are too successful, you cannot come in to serve".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think that will be a wrong principle and it is contrary to everything that made Singapore successful in the first generation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, over the years I have seen generations of Chong Pong residents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some have moved out into bigger residences, some have received scholarships to study overseas, some have moved back to stay in new developments in Nee Soon so that they could be near to take care of their ageing parents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are gratifying reminders that our system works well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have good social infrastructure to uplift those who can excel, support the vulnerable, make every town a caring and liveable home.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has been a deeply fulfilling journey for me these 35 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The heart is the same, the commitment is the same from the time when I started when I was 29.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Deputy Speaker, two clarifications about the land implications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I understand from Second Minister Edwin Tong that what is being priced in terms of square foot of built-up area is, in fact, consistent with market pricing as well as SLA's practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That said, I believe that what many Singaporeans are concerned about is this notion that when you speak of the market, there is one type of market, one class of rentals for heritage buildings with bundled land where the market valuation for land is different, and there is another market, a market where if you live in an HDB property, then it is land pricing, where otherwise you would be raiding the Reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I am wondering if, in light of this, the Second Minister wishes to comment if the SLA's anomalous approach to valuing land for black and white bungalows, if he would accept that at least there are different methodologies for the pricing of land and, if so, then will the Chief Valuer accept the possibility of differential land pricing as well for HDB?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Based on my calculations, what I found was that that would amount to, assuming a reasonable rate of interest, something in the order of $3,000 to $4,000, rather than $2,000.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I keep making this point about the market and maybe I will say that again.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You have got to look at the market.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I mentioned in my speech that we look at comparables.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You cannot take a HDB property and try and say what is the value of a black and white property for rental, based on the same principles, just as you cannot take a terrace house or a condominium and apply that as a comparable to what you do when you want to value for rental and find the right valuation for a black and white property, as we see here.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It has got to be comparable in a sense to the land size, age of the property, condition of the property, you look at the comparables and then maybe you make adjustments for outliers and for the specific condition and location of this particular property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That has been the methodology that has been used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I took some care to explain it, but now the Member, along with others, question that again; and now the Member uses the word "anomalous".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The tables that I keep going back to – I would encourage Members to please have a look at them – tell us that right across Singapore, across all different locations, where black and white bungalows can be found, for which 87% of them are managed by external professional MAs who have their own valuation teams, they assess based on market price and market methodology.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Member's point about looking at a raid on Reserves, which the Member makes it obviously to try and make the point that there is a distinction, and that the Member is trying to second guess that distinction and perhaps suggest that there are some inequality and perhaps unfair treatment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the Member will know that you got to look at it as a different comparable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: First of all, when you are valuing land for the purposes of HDB, you are looking at the question of selling HDB property with a leasehold interest of 99 years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is a very different proposition from valuing the appropriate rental to be collected from a heritage black and white property like this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yes, there are different parameters, different baskets, but that is because the intrinsic nature of the property in question calls for this difference.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Could the Member please repeat his second question?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I believe that was amortised to something in the order of $2,000 a month.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I am wondering what kind of assumptions SLA applied.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Can I ask the Member what he means by "four years"?

text: As far as I understand it, the rental was extended by a 3+2 and the time that the land clearance was implemented—

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai

text: Mr Leong, I think the Chair decides at what time the clarifications end.

text: Mr Leong, I think, the response to you is – Mr Leong, I invite you to kindly take your seat – we have had four Ministerial Statements from 12.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These are conservation properties and so there is a need to upkeep them, maintain them, based on conservation guidelines.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is a requirement on SLA, as the owner and landlord of these properties, to ensure that not just are they managed from a tenantability perspective, but also that we meet, cohere with, match up to conservation guidelines in how we maintain the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These obligations to maintain them based on conservation guidelines are on SLA, whether there is a tenant or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these are expenditures that have to be incurred to maintain the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I spent some time detailing some of the elements that we have to take into account when we maintain the property and that is irrespective of whether there is a tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But we try to do it at a time when there is going to be a confirmed tenancy so that the income stream received from the monthly rentals can go towards paying off the cost of the maintenance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is what happened in this case, for both 26 and 31 Ridout Road.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And Mr Leong Mun Wai will be aware that we have had several examples of this talked about in the media a few days ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those are all examples of properties, heritage properties, where significant expenditure was needed for the reasons that I have outlined – I would not go into it again – and which we had done over and above what Members have seen in 26 and 31 Ridout Road.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of the period of time, number of months or years that it takes to recover back, as I said, the starting point is, even if there is no tenant, you would still have to incur these expenses to upkeep, to maintain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The amount of time we take to recover, this is a factor to assess and judge whether we should proceed with this particular set of works at this time or otherwise, or maybe we can scale down or scale back if there is no tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I will take the Member's 2.2 years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You have a tenant coming in, prepared to put in enhancements like the swimming pool which, by the way, we encourage – I think the Member heard me say earlier, we encourage.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One of the ways in which SLA has been thinking of restructuring its tenancy framework is to try to encourage tenants to come in and put in capital expenditure (capex), so that these properties can both be maintained as well as enhanced for subsequent purposes.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, if a pool is there, put in at the cost of the tenant, at the expiry of the lease, that pool becomes the property of SLA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that goes towards enhancing the value of the property for subsequent tenancies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, these are factors that we take into consideration and we assess based on each individual tenant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: What do we have to do in terms of the works which we have to incur anyway?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: How can you bring it all together and ensure that we can maximise the returns?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The trees, look, if they are decayed, there is a report that the arborist puts up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in the event that the tenant does not want to take ownership of the maintenance, then that falls on SLA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If a tree falls on a neighbouring property, that is SLA's responsibility.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we take care to ensure that if the trees are found to be posing a safety concern, then we must work with the arborist, work with NParks, get the approval and then get them removed.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those are where the girth is a metre or more.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I appreciate that the Ridout Road review by Senior Minister Teo and by agencies, such as CPIB, was made at the request of Prime Minister Lee.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And I also appreciate the fact that the request for full investigation was also made by Minister Shanmugam and Minister Vivian Balakrishnan themselves to clarify that the rental transactions are aboveboard.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Since some of the Parliamentary Questions were actually directed at the Prime Minister and since the matter involves key members of the Prime Minister's Cabinet, I would like to seek Prime Minister Lee's views on the matter so far and also if he could share his views in the House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I think the focus of the debate has been on values: integrity, propriety, incorruptibility.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is no official house to live in.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is for you to judge what you need it for for your lives: save it, give it away, spend it, put in a house, travel, whatever.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, where Ministers decide to live, whether they want to rent, whether they want to buy, these are personal choices.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And thus, I see nothing wrong with Ministers renting properties from SLA or, for that matter, from a private landlord, provided it is properly done and all procedures are followed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, when I heard that two of my Ministers, Shanmugam and Vivian Balakrishnan, had rented black and white bungalows at Ridout Road, my assessment, without going into it in depth, was that I did not believe there was wrongdoing involved.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I had every confidence that my Ministers and the SLA officials who dealt with them would have done the right things and handled the rentals properly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has built up a strong reputation as an anti-corruption outfit and it has the necessary legal powers guaranteed in the Constitution to carry out a further investigation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Everybody in Singapore knows what it means when CPIB invites you to "lim kopi".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I was then in Nairobi, on an official visit to Kenya.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: CPIB's investigation went beyond the legal question of whether there was criminal conduct.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It extended to broader issues like whether there was preferential treatment enjoyed by the Ministers, whether any privilege information was disclosed to them, whether the Ministers had abused their position in the process of the rentals.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Senior Minister Teo is my most Senior Minister in terms of years in Cabinet and experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I appointed him to show that I had every intention to maintain the Government and the PAP's long-standing high and stringent standards of integrity and propriety.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I wanted to put my most experienced, most qualified, for this purpose, most capable person on the job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I did not consider Senior Minister Teo to have been involved in the transaction, even though Minister Shanmugam had informed Senior Minister Teo of the arrangements he had made to recuse himself, including that then-Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah had been told to approach Senior Minister Teo if the matter had to go beyond her.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because no such issue arose and nothing was ever raised to Senior Minister Teo.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He was the backstop – and nothing reached him.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has been suggested, including today, by some Members that even though Senior Minister Teo might not have been involved in the Ridout Road transactions, just because he is a Minister, he is not sufficiently independent to conduct this investigation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When it comes to corruption and wrongdoing, crimes, we have an independent process, as CPIB investigations are referred to the Attorney-General's Chambers for an opinion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are dealing with laws, with legality and, ultimately, the Courts are the arbiter of what is legal or illegal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But ethics and standards of propriety, those are the Prime Minister's responsibility.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have to set the standards of what is ethical, what is proper.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I cannot outsource them, for example, to appoint an ethics advisor to tell me what is proper or not proper.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have to know what is proper or not.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: An ethics advisor cannot be the one to decide and to advise the Prime Minister whether Ministers acted with propriety or not.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You have read about some of them in the newspapers over the last few months.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has not always resulted in more ethical conduct or better government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Singapore's context, the Prime Minister has to set the standards.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He issues the Rules of Prudence to PAP Members after every General Election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have done it now, I think, four times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He has to set the right personal example of proper conduct.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He decides whether a Minister has acted properly or not in accordance with a code and the rules.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If he thinks so, he should say so; if he thinks not, he must say not.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I do not wish to influence my Ministers and my Members of Parliament." Ultimately, the Prime Minister is still accountable and he has to justify his position here to Parliament and answer to Singaporeans at the ballot box.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is how it has been kept clean.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is my general approach and the attitude that I have taken in this case.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When CPIB and Senior Minister Teo submitted their reports to me, I accepted all their conclusions and ordered the reports to be published and placed before the House, before this meeting today so that everybody can read them, digest them and be ready to come here and have an informed discussion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These reports provide a good basis for Parliament to discuss the issue.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The conclusions are quite clear, as the Ministerial Statements you heard earlier have explained, from Senior Minister Teo and Second Minister Edwin Tong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The AGC confirmed this after reviewing the investigation papers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the Leader of the Opposition paid CPIB and paid the Government a compliment just now when he said nobody is suggesting corruption on the part of the Ministers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Their report explained this and CPIB established that this imprecision was not due to any ill-intent on the part of the SLA officers, nor was there any evidence of any mala fide abuse of position in the valuation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The imprecision is embarrassing to SLA and the Government, particularly as the SLA has put out a statement earlier to say that the Ministers both paid higher than the guide rents.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: CPIB calls it as it is with no regard to whom it might convenience or embarrass.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Senior Minister Teo's review relying on CPIB's findings confirm the broader issues that there was no conflict of interest or unfair advantage enjoyed and that all rules and procedures have been complied with.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And his report sets out the basis for his conclusions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are not just his personal opinions, but conclusions based on documented facts, verified and laid out in the report.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, it is very important that we have had this accounting in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members have had full opportunity to ask questions and clarify doubts.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But this accounting in Parliament is not just to resolve the issue of the rentals on two black and white properties in Ridout Road, important as that is.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is also a demonstration of how the PAP is determined to uphold the standards which it has set itself from the beginning in 1959.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This Government has not and will never tolerate any compromise or departure from the stringent standards of honesty, integrity and incorruptibility that Singaporeans expect of us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In this case, we have investigated it, the Ministers have been cleared.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In other cases which come up, we will investigate it and whichever way the facts fall out, they will be taken to their logical conclusion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is the foundation not just for the people's trust in the PAP Government, but for the integrity and good functioning of our political system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And this is my commitment and the PAP Government's unwavering commitment to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a question for the Prime Minister with regard to the scope of the CPIB investigation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Was CPIB tasked to look into the Code of Conduct for the Ministers and whether the Ministers acted in accordance to the code, because the earlier explanation of the Prime Minister suggested that CPIB looked into the whole range of issues beyond legal issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My understanding from the Miscellaneous Paper was that CPIB was looking to see whether a criminal or corruption offence could be disclosed.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And they put it into their report and in their letter to me, that they had found none of these.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He did further fact-finding on the establishment of the policies, the backgrounds and the overall way the system and SLA operated, and his conclusions are in the report.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Coming back to the gravamen of what a lot of the discussion was over the last at least three and a half hours – with regard to asking a civil servant for information – Senior Minister Teo has made his point that there was quite frankly nothing untoward about it because the nature of the information was as such.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This, of course, upon reading the Miscellaneous Paper, is not apparent to the public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is quite incongruous in the eyes of many for a Minister to be asking a civil servant details which pertain to information for his personal use.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think this is the crux of the issue.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And when people intersect it with the Ministerial Code of Conduct and your Letter of Prudence, does the Prime Minister not agree that actually this is an issue that has been flagged out and that there is a better way to address a problem of a similar nature when it crops up?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: The issue has been there since I do not know, April?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And the outrageous allegations were being made that the Ministers had enjoyed improper benefits and inside tracks and were getting a sweet deal, and all sorts of very grave innuendos were being stated.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Nobody cared how he found out about the properties.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Now that the report has come out and all those grave suspicions have been dispelled, you focus on this question and you ask should he have asked the Deputy Secretary?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My view is that he could have done it a different way, he could have done it this way.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: He has given the House the reasons why he did it this way.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think those are cogent reasons, which I accept.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: A Code of Conduct would be very relevant to establish corrupt intent.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In fact, there is a two-point rule that has been established at law.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: One is whether there has been a breach of Code of Conduct; and secondly, whether there is guilty knowledge that is associated with the action.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Deputy Speaker, I would just like to turn it back to a policy, to Second Minister Edwin Tong, and to ask if the existing policy on guide rent at the onset and upon renewal takes into consideration additional structures, like swimming pools and car porch?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because it brings additional utility; not just per se a GFA but additional utility.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And in what way does this also differ from commercial properties?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, if you are a tenant, we encourage the tenants to come and improve the facilities and make enhancements to the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all of these eventually, when it comes to a fresh tenancy, will be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You would consider this but you also consider the fact that this is the very tenant who put in the capex in the first place to bring about those enhancements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because if you did not do that and you simply at every renewal, in the 3+3+3, charge a higher rental because of what he has done, then no tenant would then eventually take this up and it would work against SLA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, with that caveat, otherwise the improvements and enhancements will be taken into account at subsequent renewals of tenancies.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And I can quite see that the amount of renovation cost that is required to be spent on rental property can be a deal breaker for many.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: So, why does SLA choose not to install modern amenities like what private landlords do to improve demand and rental rates?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But with hindsight, when it is apparent that a Minister is interested in renting the property, would it not have been better to have listed the property on SPIO?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the Member's second point, it is the call of the MA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the Member's first point about installing modern facilities, again, you got to take it in the round.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you are able to cluster them and rejuvenate and maybe invite an external private sector party to work with you to place-make and to modernise, then yes, in those cases, it has been done and we will continue on that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But obviously you do not want to install and retrofit a property in a particular way only for a tenant to want to do it in a different way.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, for some of these, we maintain it as it is, we make the basic additions from time to time, but we also rely on the tenant who comes in, such as in these two examples, to retrofit and to enhance the property.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, ask all the questions that you have.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, first of all, can I ask Second Minister Edwin Tong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think his reply is not quite complete.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Or maybe I asked the question not too well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What I was asking is: did SLA offer the same kind of package?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Did SLA offer the same kind of package to other tenants before in the rental of the black and white bungalows consisting of what I said just now, that before the tenant moved in, it coincided with the time where SLA had to refurbish the bungalow, so as a result, they spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to refurbish before the tenant moved in?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But in the past, does SLA actually allow tenants to put in swimming pools easily?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It this something that SLA really welcomed in the past?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, how do you justify that, after spending $570,000 renovating 31 Ridout Road and then, you still offer a price of $23 per square metre?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: These are my questions for Second Minister Edwin Tong.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Prime Minister, as I have said just now, we believe in the integrity of our Government led by you.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We are not against Ministers living well, living in GCBs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Although Minister Shanmugam has tried to say that we are against that just now.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But I do not think that many would disagree that, from this episode, there is a perception of an amount of conflict of interest and unfairness in the process of renting the two bungalows.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Although there may not be – and we trust the investigation by CPIB and also Senior Minister Teo – an outright misconduct of any public servant, but the result is that there is this perception there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And what the question I asked Second Minister Edwin Tong is exactly trying to drive at that – why is the package so coincidentally favourable?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, I would like to ask you one question, Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: From this episode, would you commit that from now on, the Code of Conduct of the PAP Government will be applied more stringently, learning from this episode?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You said that, "No, this episode doesn't show any shortcomings in the application of the Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: This is a kind of standard we can expect from the PAP Government", we will take it as that.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Because having said that he has nothing against Ministers living wherever they feel they wish to live, he then raises this, alleged perception of conflict of interest and unfairness, when we have spent the last five hours explaining why there is no actual conflict of interest, why potential conflicts of interest have been cut off and, therefore, there is no possibility of a reasonable perception of conflict of interest arising.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Therefore, when he says the PAP Code of Conduct, do I intend for it to be stringently applied, what he really means is, should I or should I not allow Ministers to rent GCBs or to rent Black and Whites?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: My answer is, I do not object to Ministers renting Black and Whites.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Some have come into office with means because they have had successful careers before.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: And most importantly, they continue to do their duties as a Minister and to serve their constituents and to serve Singaporeans and to make a contribution on my team, as an honest, capable – there was a phrase in the Minister's swearing-in text: "...in all things to be a true and faithful Minister." That is what we expect of all PAP Ministers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Leong, I have answered all three questions previously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I also mentioned that this is because there are conservation obligations and that is why we had appointed a consultant to advise us on what works need to be done for each of them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yes, if you would like to rent one and you want to put a pool in, we welcome that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The guide rent will assess the condition, the location, the comparables and then make a judgement on what the appropriate rental is, for that property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And in this case, you say it is below the average.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is because of the state of the condition of the property.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was in poor condition, having been vacant for about five years or so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that is a factor that the guide rent takes into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The point is that Minister Vivian Balakrishnan met the guide rent and that is why it was let to Minister Vivian Balakrishnan.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leong, could I invite you to just keep it to two clarifications?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But Minister, your answer is not logical, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And that is rent that is way below the lowest price of the range of prices in that vicinity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Do you think that is a fair price?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And if your valuation agent provided that price, do you think the SLA officials should be there to say, "No, it cannot be that price".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the final rent, in fact, it depends on this assessment, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, why did SLA not raise the objection to keep the rental price at $23 per square metre?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Leong, it is because there is a guide rent.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The guide rent is determined by an independent valuer and I would suggest not to second guess that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The whole point of appointing an MA with a valuer who looks at it independently is so that we can get an assessment, a baseline.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I thought I should answer one point that Mr Leong made, suggesting that there was a coincidence on $26,500, if I heard him right.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think he may have missed the facts when they were being set out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not know what the guide rent was.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is set out in the CPIB report and there is no coincidence in the way he suggested on $26,500.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I also set out what was the first offer I made.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: If it arises from Minister Shanmugam's response, you may proceed to ask a short clarification.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have had a long five-and-a-half hour session today dealing with the contents of the report and we have also heard from both Ministers who have leased properties from SLA, as well as a comprehensive statement from the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Therefore, just one question for the Senior Minister.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Based on the questions and views that were expressed during this very long, discussion and the clarifications, what, in the Senior Minister's opinion, are the key takeaways from the matters which have arisen in this House during these last few hours?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I appreciate the Member's question because we have had a very wide-ranging debate and I think it is useful to bring the matters to some conclusion and to be able to structure this, what we have discussed today.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Prime Minister has given a very comprehensive statement on this matter and I do not intend to make a very long winding-up.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are here because there have been allegations made against Ministers for corruption and other acts of abuse of power and so on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, this is the first issue that we have to deal with and come to a landing point on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The persons involved in the rental of these two properties understood their responsibilities to act with integrity and did so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And, Mr Deputy Speaker, this is a credit to our officers and the system as a whole.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Members have asked for many clarifications and my colleagues and I have answered all of them.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Mr Pritam Singh says no one is alleging corruption, and I am glad that he said so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is no corruption, no abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think the only remaining issue is the one of conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have explained at length what the concept of conflict of interest is, and potential conflict of interest, actual conflict of interest, and that this has been dealt with particularly in the case of Mr Shanmugam and the rental of 26 Ridout Road.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is this lingering issue of "perceived" conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And as I have explained, if we have dealt adequately and completely with a potential conflict of interest and that there has been no actual conflict of interest, then actually, a fair-minded person will come to the conclusion that, therefore, there is no basis for a perceived conflict of interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, I think this concludes the first part of our discussion.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There were a number of useful points raised regarding the management of state properties and land, in particular of black and white bungalows.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is an associated issue, and I think Second Minister Edwin Tong has explained this quite fully.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He has addressed these points and also the various suggestions that we will be looking into improving the optimisation and the use of state land, which SLA has been doing and, in particular, those which are not yet slated for redevelopment.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The second set of issues is important and it really is a reaffirmation of our collective belief in the importance of a clean Government and, for those in public service – whether elected or public officers – to act with integrity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Although the reports he received from MinLaw and SLA did not indicate a high likelihood of wrongdoing, he nevertheless directed CPIB to investigate the matter – when he was overseas – so that the matter could be examined independently and thoroughly to get to the bottom of things.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Either prove that nothing was wrong and put the allegations to rest, as we have done today, or, if the investigation turned up wrongdoing, to act on it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have come to Parliament to present the findings.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have answered the many questions and clarifications sought.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Prime Minister has spoken about the Government's commitment to integrity and the high standards in the working of Government and in our country.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: CPIB is assisted by a vigilant public and a vigilant Public Service.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is what we need in order to maintain integrity, honesty and incorruptibility in our country.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Members have made some useful comments and suggestions on the Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And as I stated earlier, we will consider, specifically, how to introduce declarations for rental property transactions for the relevant agencies and public officers dealing with land and property matters, and also have a look at this issue for Ministers and PAP Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A member of the public would be outraged and report it if a public officer were to ask him for a bribe.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: More importantly, a public officer would be outraged if he were offered a bribe and would report the person who had done so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is a virtuous circle that we must maintain and the work is never done.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I believe that this is a shared aspiration of Members from both sides of this House.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This Government is definitely dedicated to building an inclusive, progressive society.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is the driving motivation that underpins Government policies, particularly in education, housing, healthcare and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our aim is to mobilise everyone to work together, to grow the economy, to share the fruits of growth widely, to uplift the most needy among us as well as the broad mass of Singaporeans, to bridge that divide, to uplift everyone, as Minister Shanmugam said of his own experiences.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In housing, particularly, we have done more than almost any other country to secure good homes for nearly every citizen and we will ensure that there will always be sufficient and affordable HDB flats for every Singaporean household.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But at the same time, we take care to keep the right balance with a whole range of housing types.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have HDB, executive condominiums, private property and, yes, including black and white houses.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If people work hard and do well, they should be able to aspire to live in a better home in Singapore, to continue to contribute here in Singapore to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These are people in their 30s and 40s.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Many would be at the threshold where they have a good chance of reaching the peak in their chosen careers and professions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We have to bring them in and have them contributing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If they have served well, the satisfaction of having done so is the biggest reward that makes it all worthwhile.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is important so that we can build a system with a strong foundation which will help bring in good people to continue to serve in the Government to take Singapore further forward.
